answer: Each new identity has to book a measured berth at one harbor crane, hang a ferrous draft-plate whose magnetic grain is published, and settle the berth fee in a sealed saffron ampoule that is broken and assayed on receipt. Peer checkers later re-scan the plate grain and the ampoule residue. Identities that reuse one plate or one ampoule leave the same traces, are paid as a single operator, and are slashed together. Spinning up N sybils therefore costs N unique ferrous plates, N independently sourced saffron ampoules, and N non-shareable crane slots.
